History · 15 November 2026

Ebbinghaus, the man who tested himself

How a German researcher measured forgetting with nonsense syllables, and why his curve still holds.

In the 1880s Hermann Ebbinghaus set out to study memory with the rigour of physics. His problem was that words carry associations: we remember "mother" better than "screw" for reasons unrelated to time. So he invented about 2,300 meaningless syllables, such as "DAX" or "BOK".

For years he was his own only subject. He learned lists until he could recite them without error and, after a delay (twenty minutes, an hour, a day, a month), measured how much effort it took to relearn them. That saving let him calculate how much remained in memory even when he could not consciously recall it.

The curve

The result, published in 1885, was the forgetting curve: a very steep drop in the first hours and a much slower loss afterwards. He also noticed that spreading repetitions over several days worked better than massing them, the first hint of the spacing effect.

Does it hold up?

In 2015 Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros repeated the experiment with one participant who learned and relearned seventy lists. The curve closely resembled the original, with a small rise at 24 hours that they attributed to sleep.

That a single-subject experiment has stood for 130 years says a lot about how carefully it was designed. It also points to its limit: nonsense syllables are not real life, where meaning changes almost everything.

References

  1. Ebbinghaus, H. (1885). Über das Gedächtnis. Leipzig: Duncker & Humblot.
  2. Murre, J. M. J. y Dros, J. (2015). Replication and analysis of Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve. PLoS ONE, 10(7), e0120644.
